newsitem.title: CHINA: Jardine seen facing challenge under China-ruled HK.
newsitem.headline: Jardine seen facing challenge under China-ruled HK.

text.p: Just about one month after the lowering of the Union Jack in Hong Kong, Jardine Matheson, the oldest British trading group in the territory, could be facing its first challenge under Chinese rule.
Hong Kong tycoon Li Ka-shing jolted the market by retaking a stake in the Hongkong Land Holdings and another in its parent company Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd.
Through his flagship companies Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd and Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, Li acquired a 3.06 percent stake in Hongkong Land and a 3.03 percent stake in Jardine Matheson.

Jardine Matheson shares have risen about 15 percent since the announcement on Tuesday to close at US$8.10 on Thursday. Hongkong Land shares have surged 34 percent in that time, closing at US$3.42 today in Singapore.

The action raised a storm of questions. Were Cheung Kong and Hutchison Whampoa using their war chest for a renewed bid for the "Princely Hong" or trying to greenmail the largest landlord in Hong Kong's financial district?
Cheung Kong, along with several other blue-chip companies, made a raid on Hongkong Land in 1987.

The bid was unsuccessful but Jardine was forced to buy back the shares at much higher prices in the following year from the raiders who then made a gentlemen's agreement with Jardine not to attempt another takeover for seven years.
Li's elder son and vice chairman of Cheung Kong, Victor Li told reporters that the share purchase was a friendly financial investment and should not be considered a hostile move.
He declined to comment on whether the Cheung Kong group would increase its holdings in the Jardine stable.
Jardine and Matheson are names synonymous with the opium trade which led to war between Britain and China and resulted in the British seizing Hong Kong at gunpoint in 1841.

Jardine, Hong Kong's largest private sector employer, angered Beijing when it shifted its domicile from Hong Kong to Bermuda in 1984. That was the year the Sino-British declaration was signed, spelling the beginning of the end of London's 156-year rule of Hong Kong on June 30, 1997.
Shares in five of Jardine's seven listed companies have missed the Hong Kong stock market boom because their Hong Kong listings were withdrawn at the end of 1994 and in 1995.
Wen Wei Po, a Beijing-controlled newspaper in Hong Kong, said on Wednesday that Cheung Kong seemed to be interested in Jardine's Hong Kong properties and not in a takeover.
"The possibility of a hostile takeover bid is non-existent," it said in an editorial, pointing to Jardine's anti-takeover mechanism which was put in place after the 1987 raid.
Wen Wei Po said Jardine had misjudged post-handover Hong Kong and now was trying to re-establish ties to the territory.
Jardine Matheson has said it welcomed Cheung Kong's recent investment in its companies.
"We are pleased that they recognise good value in Jardine Matheson and Hongkong Land," Jardine Matheson's managing director Alasdair Morrison told Reuters on Tuesday.
The Cheung Kong group was just one of the hidden Jardine stakeholders to come to light recently.
In a notice to the Singapore Stock Exchange earlier this year, Hongkong Land said Gainluck Co Ltd had acquired more than three percent of the company.
Gainluck is controlled by the family Ho Ying-kit, the owner of HK Tobacco Co Ltd.

The Ho family owns five to eight percent of Hongkong Land and was considering lifting the stake to 10 percent, the Hong Kong Economic Journal on Thursday quoted a source close to the family as saying.
He said the family bought the shares through three companies and this was just one item in its investment portfolio.

The Ho family is well regarded by the mainland Chinese government, and Charles Ho, a grandson of Ho Ying-kit and the family's investment manager, helped select Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, the newspaper said.

Stocks analysts said it was natural for China to want to see Hong Kong's central business district come under a Hong Kong Chinese company's control and the Cheung Kong acquisition could yield cooperation between Cheung Kong and Jardine in the future.
Hongkong Land owns five million square feet of prime office and retail space in the main business district, housing some of Hong Kong's classiest stores -- Tiffany's, Gucci and Vuitton.
